report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The concept of Umwelt refers to the phenomenal world of an organism, defined by its senses and what it does to stay alive, thrive and reproduce.

Umwelt had a powerful influence on how the scientific study of animal behavior under natural conditions developed in the middle decades of the 20th century and currently is enjoying renewed interest in the field of comparative cognition.
Traditionally, animals have been the exclusive focus of Umwelt-based analysis.
This chapter focuses on Myxococcus xanthus, a predatory bacterium with an unusual, complex social lifestyle.

The presentation is intended to show that the Umwelt concept can be useful in unpacking, in radically alien forms of life, processes regarded as cognitive in animals and in a context (predator-prey interactions) long important to ethology and comparative psychology, where Umwelt has done most work.

Whatever its true affinities may prove to be...the order Myxobacteriaceae is undeniably a very interesting and important one, and although the present account is necessarily incomplete, it may serve to call attention to a subject which, beyond question, offers a productive field for further investigation.

Roland Thaxter (1892; pp.393-4) A concept for connecting the dots in an evolutionary science of cognition For the past several years I and others have been arguing for the utility of basal cognition for understanding the evolution of biological capacities typically associated with mentality [see, in particular, special issues of Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2021, vol. 376, issues 1820 and 1821) and the special article collection in Animal Cognition ].

text.text: These capacities include differential responding to signs and cues, memory, appetitive and aversive responses (valence), learning, decision making, error correction, anticipation/prediction, and communication.
"Basal" here mirrors usage in evolutionary biology.
'Basal metazoans' refers to the earliest evolved constitutively multicellular organisms known as animals.

A more-or-less traceable continuum is assumed to exist on a variety of levels between basal metazoans and animals with nervous systems, as well as between animals with simple nervous systems and animals with highly complex brains.
Basal cognition hypothesizes that a more-or-less traceable continuum exists in a basic toolkit of behaviorgenerating cognitive capacities found in microbes to Homo sapiens (Lyon et al., 2021).

text.text: I define cognition as the processes by which an organism becomes familiar with, values, and exploits or evades features of its environment to meet existential goals (e.g., survival, wellbeing, reproduction) (Lyon et al., 2021).
text.formatted: I define cognition as the processes by which an organism becomes familiar with, values, and exploits or evades features of its environment to meet existential goals (e.g., survival, wellbeing, reproduction) <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Lyon et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: How these basic capacities are realized in different types of organism varies markedly in complexity and flexibility-the result of evolutionary history, ecology, ways of life (solitary, social), and so on-albeit with many common features, functionally and mechanistically.
All are tools evolved for adaptation, serving lived imperatives.

The most successful approach for uncovering fundamental processes in the life sciences for the past century has been to start with the simplest tractable model system, derive principles, then scale up to more complex instances.

This is not often because the phenomena of interest were first identified in these simple models-such phenomena are typically common to life-but because the physiological complexity of the animals in which they did first attract and hold attention, including humans, is so great as to inhibit understanding.

The logic of transgenerational trait transmission was first inferred in pea plants, the physical basis of biological inheritance discovered in bacteria, the basic elements of genetic expression learned in fruit flies, and the findings applied to more complex animals, including us.

This start simple-derive principles-scale up methodology provided fundamental insights into the energetic economy of organisms (respiration), the mechanism of ion channels (the basis of bioelectricity), physiological regulation in adverse conditions (e.g., stress responses), signal transduction, sensorimotor behavior, development, and much more.
For instance, the current leading molecular model for investigating the mechanism by which anaesthesia works its wondrous effects in animals is, in fact, bacterial (Nury et al., 2011).

text.text: There is no principled reason why this approach shouldn't apply to constrained, well-defined issues in comparative cognition and psychology.

In this chapter I will show how a conceptual framework introduced more than a century ago by an Estonian-German aristocrat, Jakob Johann von Uexküll (1909), can be a useful tool for getting a grip on the phenomenon of predation, a behavior typically considered cognitive in animals, in a way that could productively contribute to a deeply evolutionary, phyletically more inclusive comparative science of cognition and behavior.
text.formatted: In this chapter I will show how a conceptual framework introduced more than a century ago by an Estonian-German aristocrat, Jakob Johann von <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Uexküll (1909)</ref>, can be a useful tool for getting a grip on the phenomenon of predation, a behavior typically considered cognitive in animals, in a way that could productively contribute to a deeply evolutionary, phyletically more inclusive comparative science of cognition and behavior.

text.text: The central concept of this framework is Umwelt, literally "surrounding world".

In von Uexküll's usage, Umwelt refers not to the environment (Umbegung) as commonly understood 1 but, rather, to the phenomenal world of an organism generated by its sensory capacities in contact with features of its surroundings (Gamble, 1910).

That said, 'environmental protection' in German is Umweltschutz.
The term phenomenology is used here in its established scientific sense, as it was by von Uexküll.
In physics, phenomenology refers to models or descriptions that capture observable regularities without specifying underlying mechanisms.
In biology it refers to the systematic description of observable organism-level dynamics independent of specific mechanistic accounts.

Phenomenological descriptions characterize the organized appearance of biological processes at the scale where functional coherence emerges, while mechanistic explanations account for their realization.
The two are complementary rather than competing explanatory modes.

This usage differs profoundly from philosophical phenomenology concerned with firstperson subjective experience, which is not what von Uexküll, a marine biologist (albeit a philosophical one), was concerned with when he introduced the concept.
Umwelt denotes the organism-environment coupling that gives rise to functional perceptual worlds, species-specific meaning structures, and perception-action loops.

As per Lewontin, environment here does not mean external sets of circumstances acting upon passive living systems but, rather, milieux actively constructed and modified by organisms in a reciprocal causal relationship that shapes selection and behavior (Lewontin, 2000).

text.text: Organism and environment co-define, or co-construct, one another.
This perspective aligns closely with von Uexküll's, but does not stand in for it, because Lewontin does not privilege perception.
Perceptual capacities, action systems, and environmental structure are all critical for niche construction, another important concept in comparative cognition and psychology.
A niche encompasses all the interactions an organism has as it makes a living, including food sources, habitat, activity patterns, and reproductive strategies.
Niche construction emphasizes organism modification of environmental conditions through their activities and metabolism.
Essentially, they construct the environment they not only experience but for which they are evolved by natural selection (Scott-Phillips et al., 2014).

text.text: Such knowledge interpreted in the context of valid scientific understanding about human phenomenology and behavior (as against unverified subjective first-person imputation) has been shown to be capable of yielding productive cognitive insights in non-traditional, poorly understood and under-studied animal models (e.g., snakes and other reptiles), paradigmatically in Burghardt's own work.

The aim of this chapter is to provide a glimpse of how an even more radically non-traditional, aneural model organism may nevertheless shed new light on long-standing issues in these comparative cognition-related fields: predator-prey behavior, collective dynamics, and eusociality.

text.text: Focusing on the predatory behavior of M. xanthus helps to limit the discussion to an area with analogs in more familiar forms of life.

Von Uexküll illustrated his ideas with the reproductive lifecycle of a female castor bean tick (Iodes ricinus), presented in a sequence of three functional circles involving different sensory modalities and sets of effectors (2010).
In functional circle #1 the tick is poised, clinging, on a blade of grass or a bough, awaiting the chemical sign of butyric acid, exuded by mammalian skin.
When butyric acid is sensed, the tick releases its grip and falls.
So ends functional circle #1.
If the tick falls onto something warm, ascertained by temperature sensors, functional circle #2 begins.
(If it does not, the tick ascends a new perch.)
On the warm surface of the host's body the arachnid begins searching for a hairless spot on the skin.

Once located, the tick uses its mouth to cut into the flesh to reach blood, releasing saliva to both numb the spot (staving off host expulsion efforts) and prevent clotting, then inserts a feeding tube.
Feeding may last several days.
Functional circle #3 begins when distention of the tick's body is such that it stops sucking blood.
The engorged tick detaches from the host and drops off.
If the tick is an adult female that has mated, she lays eggs (thousands), to be nourished by the blood she holds.
She then dies.
The primary signs constitutive of the tick Umwelt in von Uexküll's account are three: butyric acid (chemical), temperature, and mechanical distention.
(Lack of obstruction by hair is arguably a fourth.)
Today, the Umwelt of a tick looks more complex.

Ticks produce and respond to a wide variety of chemical signals (Sonenshine, 2006), and respond differentially according to their current state in the present context, which includes nutritive status and lifecycle stage (larvae, nymph, adult) (Tsunoda, 2008).

text.text: The Umwelt of M. xanthus, an organism that lives, hunts, kills, feeds, reproduces and sporulates in the microscopic domain, is nowhere near as neat as the castor bean tick's, not least because the ability to observe what it is doing at an individual level is so much more problematic.
The M. xanthus lifecycle is relentlessly predatory, intensely social, intimately cooperative, indeed multicellular.

The rod-shaped bacterium hunts collectively, preys and consumes collectively, then constructs extraordinary 3-dimensional, spore-containing structures that will seed the next population when conditions improve.
On any measure, this bacterium has a more behaviorally complex lifecycle than von Uexküll's tick, which possesses central and peripheral nervous systems.
This suggests a more complicated Umwelt, arguably much more complicated.
A word about multicellularity: All multicellular organisms are made up of individual cells.
Obligate multicellularity is what plants and animals display; they are whole organisms made up of individual cells that perform specialized jobs within the system.
In tissue each cell is obliged to act with the ones that surround it because they are physically connected to one anotherobliged, except in the case of programmed cell death and cancer.

Facultative multicellularity, exhibited by M. xanthus and other unicellular organisms, is the self-organization of individual cells into structured collectives to perform important tasks (e.g., predation, sporulation, biofilm construction).
They behave like multicellular organisms.
A technical point before we proceed.
The literature on the mechanisms of M. xanthus behavior is highly technical, expressed in a blizzard of acronyms associated with proteins and genes.
Umwelt analysis, by contrast, always begins with a phenomenal description of behavior, which defines the territory in which investigation proceeds.
I have aimed here to paint a picture of M. xanthus behavior in broad brush strokes in language comprehensible to a non-specialist reader, in the context of von Uexküll's idea of a functional circle.
The details are fascinating, however.
History is being made in the exploration of this efficient killer as I write these words.

text.text: Regardless of its ecological role, rippling is a striking transition in collective behavior involving the directed movement of very large numbers of cells preparatory to multicellular development.
Collective development in Myxococcus xanthus has long been associated with starvation, historically the experimental condition used to induce multicellular development in the laboratory.

Rippling, a highly energetic phenomenon, may be understood as a transitional collective regime arising due to changes in organism-environment interaction, or shifts in the salience of factors constituting the Umwelt.

Despite truly groundbreaking research into the complex cooperative lifecycle and unusual behavior of M. xanthus, particularly in the last two decades, huge knowledge gaps remain, especially concerning what the bacterium is capable of sensing, by what means, and how this affects behavior.

Until relatively recently the behavior of individual M. xanthus cells was little studied in depth, due largely to a strong focus on collective developmental behaviors combined with inadequate means for observing single-cell behavior, but this deficit is being corrected rapidly and dramatically with major advances in imaging methods (Arend et al., 2021; Dinet et al., 2021; Herrou et al., 2024; Herrou et al., 2025; Rombouts, 2021; Rombouts et al., 2023; Seef et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020).

text.text: Outlining the contours of the M. xanthus Umwelt thus often depends on data on social behaviors, not individual capacities, including sensing and signaling the nature of which cannot yet be specified.

The aim here, however, is solely to show how analytical methods that have guided the study of cognitively driven behavior in animals can apply to certain bacteria in the context of basal cognition as a project for connecting the dots in the evolution of cognition.
The phenomenological data available is more than adequate for this purpose, despite the shortcomings.

In M. xanthus efficient predation is a profoundly collective affair that depends fundamentally on distributed, population-level coordination of individual behavior-similar to animals that herd, flock and shoal-using the most complex system of locomotion yet discovered in a bacterium.
This paradigm-shattering, dual-mechanism motility system defied explanation until this century.
Improvements in microscopy and imaging methods enabled rapid progress.

Several recent discoveries (Gloag et al., 2016; Han et al., 2025; Mas et al., 2025; Saulnier et al., 2024) are transforming the traditional picture of M. xanthus motility in unexpected ways that bring Umwelt, Lewontin's co-construction hypothesis and niche construction to the fore.

text.text: Functional circle #1: Foraging and collective predation 1.
Hunting prey: scouting and swarming M. xanthus moves across solid surfaces using two distinct but coordinated motility systems.
These systems allow cells to glide without flagella and to organize into highly structured swarms capable of efficient collective predation.

The two mechanisms-A-motility (adventurous) and S-motility (social)-operate through different physical interactions with the environment but share a common regulatory architecture that allows cells to switch direction and reorganize dynamically within a moving group (Mas et al., 2025; Saulnier et al., 2024).

text.text: A-motility allows individual cells to move independently.
The mechanism depends on distributed focal adhesion-like complexes that couple intracellular motors to transient attachment points along the cell body.
In this system, a motor complex transmits force to adhesion proteins that anchor briefly to the substrate (Mignot et al., 2007).

text.text: A-motility supports exploratory movement of individual cells or loosely packed groups, particularly during colony expansion and early encounters with prey.
S-motility commonly operates in large groups of cells (Hu et al., 2011)  7 and depends on type IV pili, long retractable filaments that extend from the leading cell pole.

text.text: Type IV pili comprise an ancient nanomachine that has been dubbed "the prokaryotic Swiss Army knife" (Berry & Pelicic, 2014) due to the myriad critical uses to which it has been put in widely differing species.

text.text: In S-motility the filaments function like molecular grappling hooks.
The pili are extended from the leading pole and attach to nearby material-substrate, neighboring cells, and environmental objects-and then retracted, pulling the cell forward (Wu et al., 2009).

text.text: Pili-mediated pulling works most effectively in dense populations where attachment opportunities are abundant.
S-motility is known to promote coordinated group movement and helps maintain alignment within swarms (Kaiser, 2008).

text.text: For many decades the two motility systems were assumed to operate separately in largely different contexts: A-motility for solitary cells and S-motility for dense swarms.
Recent work combining enhanced imagining techniques and video has overturned this view.
The first major discovery was that cells seamlessly switch between scouting and swarming (Rombouts et al., 2023).

text.text: In follow-up work, using detailed single-cell tracking and focusing on behavior at the boundary of swarming and rippling, Mas and colleagues (Mas et al., 2025) show that both propulsion systems can operate simultaneously within the same cell.

text.text: Wild type cells possessing both motors exhibit a distinct movement signature and are capable of locomotion twice as fast as genetic knock-out mutants with only one modality.
This demonstrates that co-deployment generates enhanced locomotor capacity rather than simple redundancy.
Cells at the boundaries between different collective dynamics (swarming and rippling), which manifest in adjacent patches of the moving mass, shifted easily between them.
The finding also implies that motility is tunable and that cells adjust the relative contribution of the two propulsion systems depending on environmental conditions.
Movement in M. xanthus is not continuous in one direction.
Cells periodically reverse their polarity, causing the leading and trailing poles to exchange roles, which reverses travelling direction.
Functionally, this produces something analogous to the run-and-tumble logic of flagellated bacteria, to keep the organism from traveling too far off-piste, although by a very different mechanism.
Rather than tumbling to reorient in liquid, M. xanthus reverses direction on a surface.
This process is governed by a regulatory system centered on the proteins MglA/MglB and the Frz chemosensory pathway.

MglA localizes to the leading cell pole and promotes assembly of motility machinery, while Frz signaling periodically triggers reversals that relocate MglA-and the motility complexes-to the opposite pole (Dinet et al., 2021).

text.text: Both mechanisms are sensitive to environmental cues.
Han and colleagues in the Shaevitz lab (2025) show that thin M. xanthus colonies contain transient patches of cells moving in the same direction, a phenomenon they term local polar order.

By measuring cell orientation, velocity, polarity, and substrate forces simultaneously, they demonstrate that these polar domains generate large traction-force fluctuations that cannot be explained in terms of the characteristic parallel alignment of M. xanthus where local polar order is not maintained.
Crucially, the magnitude of this polar order is controlled by cell reversal frequency.

When reversals become less frequent, polar domains persist longer, mechanical stresses increase, and cells begin to stack into additional layers, necessary for building the 3-dimensional structures of later developmental stages.

The study therefore identifies a direct physical mechanism linking polarity dynamics, collective motion, and colony morphogenesis, showing that changes in behavioral interaction dynamics can trigger major structural transitions in the colony without a change in genetic instructions.
A small shift in behavioral timing changes the interaction field, which reorganizes the system, much as collisions do in a crowd.foot_3

As colonies move across surfaces they also construct a complex extracellular milieu that facilitates gliding and much more.

This extracellular matrix includes self-produced exopolysaccharides (EPS), which combines with constituents of killed prey and self-produced outer membrane vesicles (OMVs), pouches of organic materials pinched off from the cell's outer membrane typically containing proteins and nucleic acids.

text.text: Although M. xanthus is an efficient predator, it is not the speediest bacterium on the block.
Indeed, it moves at almost glacial speed.

The average M. xanthus vegetative cell is 5-10 µm (micrometres, or thousandths of a millimetre) long and ~0.5 µm wide, with a gliding speed-in two-dimensions on solid surfaces-of 4-7 µm per minute (Patra et al., 2016).

text.text: Together A-motility, S-motility, extracellular structuring, and reversal control produce the large-scale behavior known as swarming.
Densely packed cells move outward in coordinated sheets that explore surfaces and initiate predation.
Under certain conditions-as cell density increases during prey consumption-these dynamics can shift into rippling, the next functional circle.
As we have seen, the underlying motility machinery remains active throughout this transition (Saulnier et al., 2024).

text.text: Individual cells appear capable of toggling between locomotor regimes depending on environmental conditions, including cues generated by the colony itself during migration and predation.

Through motility M. xanthus cells continuously modify the conditions that shape their own subsequent behavior in ways that feed back into the dynamics of behavior and collective organization, including morphogenesis.
Self-production of cues that guide subsequent action is a characteristic of niche construction.

Locating and utilizing prey in this functional circle is critically dependent upon adventurous cells, which alone or in small numbers act as lethal scouts (Seef et al., 2021), striking out beyond the boundaries of the mass of cells which form the main predatory force (Rombouts, 2021; Rombouts et al., 2023).

text.text: Now we move into opaque territory: the bacterium's sensorium.
M. xanthus' genome enables no fewer than eight chemotaxis systems similar to those originally discovered in flagellated bacteria, which use them to sense the environment and drive motility.
In the early 1980s, M. xanthus was tested across a wide range of substances well known to attract and repel swimming bacteria.

The myxobacterium failed to respond, suggesting a lack of capacity for chemotaxis-as-we-know-it (Dworkin & Eide, 1983), even as it responded to chemically inert objects (latex or glass beads) in ways other bacteria do not (Dworkin, 1983). 10 Researchers suggested M. xanthus' seeming chemotactic incompetence might be due to the vastly different time scales on which it moves relative to prey.

text.text: Of the eight chemotaxis systems in the M. xanthus genome, only two-Frz and Dif-have been characterized to a satisfying degree.
Both are sensitive to environmental cues and population density.
The sensing target of Frz, which regulates polarity switching and cell reversals, is unclear.

While the Frz system is not classically chemotactic in structure, or entirely in output, it has the capacity for signal amplification, signal integration and nonlinear responses to stimulation (Bretl & Kirby, 2016) that have been counted among the "cognitive features" typical of chemotactic systems (Lyon, 2015).

This refractory period acts as a memory of the last cell reversal.

text.text: Chemical signals are secreted and diffuse into the environment.
When a threshold density of signal is detected, cells collectively alter gene expression and engage in new behaviors.
M. xanthus has toxin-antitoxin systems that would immunize itself and its siblings from the adverse effects of its own poisons if secreted in this manner.
Convincing evidence did not follow, however.

text.text: The precise antibiotic(s) M. xanthus uses in the Kil system are unknown.

While Kil is sufficient to kill prey, it does not fully lyse the cell to release nutritive contents for consumption, which is accomplished by another, multitasking molecular apparatus similar to a Type-III secretion system.
Kil system proteins form where contact occurs between M. xanthus and prey cell.
At the contact site a filamentous Kil pilus, a mechanism for transferring toxic agents, is constructed and inserted into the prey cell.

Genetic evidence shows the killing function of this major pilus is linked to four minor pilin complexes that appear to form "interchangeable 'Tips'", which work in combination "to detect and kill phylogenetically diverse bacterial species" (Herrou et al., 2025; p.1).

One size doesn't fit all, because it doesn't have to.

text.text: Functional circle #2 begins when M. xanthus invades a prey colony sufficiently abundant to trigger large-scale reorganization of motility, predation/consumption, and reproduction in a visually arresting phenomenon called rippling.

As Berleman and colleagues observe: "Rippling behavior coordinates cell movement across areas of several square millimeters and can involve >10 8 cells working as a unit" (Berleman et al., 2008; p. 17127)-an extraordinary feat of coordination by any measure.

text.text: These striking collective patterns pose a long-standing problem familiar to the study of animal cognition: How can coordinated collective behavior, in this case facultative multicellular organization, arise in the absence of centralized control?
Quorum sensing long seemed to be the answer.
Rippling was believed, based on mutant studies, to be driven by C-signal-mediated regulation of reversal frequency.

While C-signaling clearly contributes to coordination, the precise mechanism by which large-scale waves arise nevertheless remained unresolved, although it was becoming increasingly evident that cell alignment is critical (Zhang et al., 2012), including, in the case of C-signaling, pole to pole alignment (Farrugia et al., 2025; Kaiser, 2004).

text.text: New research provides a unifying explanation for this long-standing puzzle, but not in the way long expected.

Recent work by the Mignot lab, using combined experimental observation and modelling, show that transitions between swarming and rippling can arise from local interaction dynamics rather than from changes in genetic regulation or specialized signaling programs (Saulnier et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Recent work by the Mignot lab, using combined experimental observation and modelling, show that transitions between swarming and rippling can arise from local interaction dynamics rather than from changes in genetic regulation or specialized signaling programs <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Saulnier et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The key observation is that cells preferentially reverse direction in regions where their forward movement becomes constrained by the surrounding collective.
In dense populations, collisions and alignment forces often prevent cells from moving along their preferred trajectories.

This mismatch between intended and realized motion is quantified as a "frustration index": reversals occur disproportionately in the most frustrated regions of the swarm, where individual movement is most constrained.
In practical terms, this means that rippling emerges as cells continuously negotiate local traffic conditions created by their neighbours and the extracellular environment.

When congestion increases-particularly in areas with significant quantities of prey cells, alive or dead-cells reverse more frequently, generating oscillatory waves that propagate through the population.

Crucially, these patterns do not require genetic reprogramming or centralized signaling: they arise from the modulation of reversal dynamics and the tunable refractory period governing when a cell can reverse again (Saulnier et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Crucially, these patterns do not require genetic reprogramming or centralized signaling: they arise from the modulation of reversal dynamics and the tunable refractory period governing when a cell can reverse again <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Saulnier et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Collective patterning thus reflects the regulation of interaction constraints within the swarm itself, transforming what might otherwise be chaotic crowding into ordered, travelling waves of coordinated motion.
Seen through the lens of Umwelt, this finding is particularly illuminating.
The bacterium's functional circle is not defined solely by internal regulatory programs but by the relational field created by neighbouring cells, extracellular matrices, and prey-derived substrates.

Saulnier and colleagues show that different environmental structures impose distinct alignment regimes on moving cells: short-range alignment along extracellular slime trails promotes swarming, whereas long-range alignment within prey-derived matrices favours rippling (Saulnier et al., 2024).

text.text: The same organism, deploying different facets of the same motility machinery, generates different collective behaviors because the structure of its world changes.
The environment is not merely a background condition but an active constraint field shaping the organism's available actions and the organization of its behavior.
How precisely the relative abundance of prey cells affects the mix-beyond the obvious fact that it does-is yet to be determined.
This perspective aligns closely with Lewontin's argument that organisms and environments are mutually constructed rather than independently specified.

In predatory swarms of M. xanthus extracellular matrix, inscribed furrows, lysed prey, and dense cell populations continuously reshape the physical and informational landscapes in which subsequent behavior unfolds.

Rippling can thus be understood as an emergent regulatory regime within this co-constructed environment-one that redistributes resources, maintains coordinated interaction, and stabilizes collective organization during periods of declining but still exploitable nutrients.

In niche-construction terms, the bacterial community actively generates the very environmental structures that organize its own activity, illustrating how organism-environment coupling can produce complex behavioral order without the need for centralized control or new genetic programs.
In sum, imaging at the single-cell level demonstrates that collective reorganization by rippling emerges from congestion-related reversal dynamics.

Whatever the role of specific chemical signals or external gradients may prove to be-and they may be substantial-the mechanical forces of congestion arising from organism-environment relations may prove to be the dominant perceptual constraint shaping collective action in this stage.

In Umwelt terms, congestion becomes a dominant perceptual cue within the functional circle of rippling, which reorganizes collective behavior through altered possibilities for action rather than through new internal programs.
Multiple functional circles exist after rippling and commencement of the decline of available prey, with starvation the inevitable result.
These involve even more dramatic multicellular behavior, which cannot be addressed here.
The declining prey environment restructures the Umwelt, directing activity toward aggregation and sporulation.
The following, briefly, is the sequence of events.
First, reproduction is down-regulated and aggregation begins.

Likened to the great animal herd migrations of the Serengeti in Africa (Shimkets, 1999), many hundreds of thousands of cells come together, first to form large mounds and then organized, dropletshaped, 3-dimensional structures called fruiting bodies.

text.text: Inside the fruiting bodies, about 10% of the rod-shaped cells transform into round, more compact myxospores.
Outside the fruiting bodies, another 20-30% of the population transform into peripheral rods, so-called because they form around the periphery of the fruiting bodies.
Peripheral rods are also metabolically down-regulated, although not as stringently as myxospores, and are unresponsive to an endogenous signal associated with sporulation.
The remaining cells in the population-the overwhelming majority-autocide: 13 they lyse themselves.

The prevailing consensus (although not universally accepted) is that this phenomenon is what it appears to be-altruistic sacrifice-to ensure the energetically demanding sporulation process is completed despite vanishing nutrients (Popp & Mascher, 2019).

text.text: In the M. xanthus case, a small minority of the population is preserved, growth can begin anew when conditions improve, and the colony continues.
How autocide is induced, however, remains unclear.
The first thing we can say with confidence about the phenomenal world of M. xanthus is that it is truly social, or eusocial.
Every facet of its existence, including (very probably) feeding, 14 is lived in groups in which an individual cell's behavior intimately affects and is affected by others.

This is not to say that M. xanthus meets most modern definitions of eusociality in evolutionary biology, which are derived exclusively from animals (ants, some bees, termites, some vertebrates) and which, in keeping with the Modern Synthesis, measures the phenomenon entirely in terms of reproduction, especially reproductive castes (Crespi & Yanega, 1995), which does not (so far) apply in prokaryotes.

The reason why this is important is because, as we know from extensive work in animals, eusociality has consequences for the kinds of sensing and behavior of which an organism is capable; also, discernible patterns exist in that way of life.
A prominent pattern is the tight, colony-level co-regulation of physiology and behavior at the molecular level (Friedman et al., 2020), which is everywhere apparent in M. xanthus.

text.text: Another is the necessity for tracking mechanisms in predatory eusocial species.
We have already seen that a derivative of the M. xanthus chemoattractant PE is found in tracking mechanisms in eukaryotes, including social amoeba, phagocytic human immune cells, and omnivorous ants.
From a basal cognition perspective, this would suggest that a closer look at PE-following in those distant phyla may hold clues for understanding aspects of M. xanthus behavior.
Convergent evolution repeatedly shows that similar problems in making a living in particular ways are often solved in broadly similar fashion.
So, is eusociality a fair ascription?
As we have seen, M. xanthus is a form of cellular life that lives very much as a collective, functioning in many respects like a dynamically motile tissue.

There are no observations, there is no literature, on the behavior of free-living M. xanthus, unlike in D. discoideum, in which the developmental cycle begins with the aggregation of free-living amoeba (Annesley & Fisher, 2009).

text.text: Starvation signaling brings these solitary predators together for multicellular transformation and sporulation.
M. xanthus, by contrast, appears to be effectively involved in functionally collective behavior at every life stage.
Whether solitary, A-motile M. xanthus cells can sustain themselves without group support, given the proportion of the nutrient load they leave behind after killing, is arguably an open question.
However, periodic reversals keep them close to the larger group. 15 Close observation of M. xanthus under ecologically valid conditions is necessary.

text.text: Also supporting the ascription of eusociality is the high degree to which cells tend to align themselves body-to-body and end-to-end, which very likely facilitates the intimate cell-to-cell exchange of existentially important goods of various kinds.
Other indications of eusociality are rippling and how multicellular development proceeds.
Killing is what M. xanthus does, relentlessly, but feeding and reproduction for reproduction's sake is not the sole driver of the behavior: continuation of the colony appears to be.
Large-scale autocide of most of the (recently acquired) population during multicellular development is only the most shocking piece of evidence for such an ascription.
Population numbers must be high enough to engage in sporulation; rippling may have a key role in accomplishing this.
M. xanthus may thus provide a useful testbed for evolutionary theories of group-level adaptation in superorganisms (Gardner & Grafen, 2009; Wilson & Hölldobler, 2005).

text.text: If prey is declining, starvation and population collapse will follow.
Starvation would be too late, although there is evidence M. xanthus cells store lipid bodies, 16 which would be an anticipatory behavior analogous to storing fat.

Similarly, in E. coli, the transition from aerobic to anaerobic respiration, necessary to survive the oxygen-free environment of the stomach and intestines, begins immediately upon a rise in ambient temperature from entering the body of an animal host (Tagkopoulos et al., 2008).

text.text: By the time the bacterium hits the stomach, it's too late to make the switch.

What we don't know is how M. xanthus detects a step-down in prey availability, which would seem to require the kind of tunable sensitivity to something in the surroundings that chemotaxis systems evolved to do.
Whether PE-sensing and Dif are involved, or something else-something more indirect but accurate and predictive of where circumstances are heading-remains to be seen.

Perhaps the M. xanthus sensorium remains obscure because much of it operates quite differently from the paradigms on offer, and that might be because its priorities, as a form of life, are also quite different from the norm.
On the other hand, M. xanthus has not been studied as intensively as other bacterial model systems and what is obscure could perhaps be explained more classically than expected.

In this chapter I have sketched in broad brush strokes the complex behavior of the beautifully contrarian, relentlessly predatory bacterium M. xanthus in the context of von Uexküll's concepts of Umwelt and functional circle, Lewontin's co-construction hypothesis and niche construction.
In the process I have noted capacities and mechanisms that function in the 16 Thanks to a reviewer for this observation.

behavior of the myxobacterium but also in the cognitively driven behavior of eukaryotes, including animals, the kinds of signs required for a connecting-the-dots analysis in basal cognition.

These include: (1) stigmergy; (2) deceptive signaling; (3) the capacity to eavesdrop on prey species via secreted chemical signals never meant for M. xanthus; (4) chemoattraction to a phospholipid that is also an attractant to predatory eukaryotic cells; and (5) a sense of touch, used in killing and possibly physiological co-regulation and cooperative behavior.
Much remains to be revealed about how this 'simple' myxobacterium does everything it can do.
There is much here that conforms to the literature on predator-prey interactions in comparative cognition and comparative psychology as well as behavioral ecology.
In the microworld, too, the evolutionary arms race between predator and prey is apparent, as prey species evolve defences against this apex predator of the prokaryotic realm.

Bacillus subtilis, another sporulating bacterium that exhibits complex multicellular behavior, has evolved a toxin to retard the predatory onslaught of M. xanthus and can construct resilient megastructures to keep it at bay (Müller et al., 2016).

Biological behavior discharges some aspect of a goal state induced simultaneously by elements external to the living system and elements internal to the organism.

The phenomenal domain where the inner world intersects with the world beyond the organism's boundary-the living process that interprets what is happening given the available cues, and what needs to happen given the organism's current state-constitutes the Umwelt.

An organism's relations to its surroundings, which define its Umwelt, can be inferred from the kinds of things (i.e., signs and cues) an organism can sense and the behavioral effects of perception in the context of function.
No organism can sense and respond to-or needs to sense and respond toeverything in its environment.

What it can sense and respond to, therefore, provides information about the organism: how it makes a living, what it does, what it can do and, hypothetically, what it may be able to do in novel circumstances.
